items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-08-23
items.q: he stayed at the Dewdrop Hotel because that's where he was playing with Frank Pannier. When Frank was the modern-day technician of the South who promoted for the first time...

ctx.x: Because this was what you would call spiritual rejuvenation. A lot of people didn't understand what was happening with the blues, especially some of the white bands who just started picking up on the blues into the late 80s, that the blues really came out of the black church. And, well, prior to that, the sacrifices that blacks made were harmed from the soul because they paid so many dues. And then, as I talked with my old great uncles from way back when they spoke with their ancestors and relatives during the…
Did that cause the demise of that club? Because I don't think it...

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: I was talking about Charlie Rosenthal over in Orange, Texas, who was a good friend of Frank Pannier. Both of them were very good promoters. And since the Dewdrop had developed an image factor worldwide right after World War II, because he brought in, Frank brought in so much live entertainment... Fr

ctx.x: So you must have been out all night.

No, I had traveled quite a bit. See, at that time, I was working for a brown, brown, see, that was a liquor company. You know, this old, old Forrester, and early times, and King Liquor at that time. And I used to travel all through Louisiana and part of Texas. If you notice, I have a lot, a lot about Texas in here, about, well, Forrestal, what is the name, Rosenthal out of Orange, Texas, who was a big time promoter. He and Frank Pannier, they were co-promoters on shows from New Orleans all the way over to Orange,…
I'm just curious stuff about Butch Curran, about the traveling, about writing the column and so forth. Go and put your date on it again and put your billboard on it.
